newsitem.title: BULGARIA: BULGARIA GRAPPLES WITH ENERGY CRISIS.
newsitem.headline: BULGARIA GRAPPLES WITH ENERGY CRISIS.

text.p: SOFIA, Sept 26 (Reute) - Debt-ridden Bulgaria, heavily dependent on its nuclear power plant at Kozloduy, this winter will rely on coal imports to replace idle reactor, but energy officials said there may be power cuts nevetheless.

Kozloduy, a Soviet-designed nuclear station on the river Danube, has closed its oldest reactor in May for safety tests under pressure from the European Union, concerned over the safety of its vessel's metal.

The National Electricity Company (NEC) chairman Kozma Kuzmanov said the 440-megawatt reactor would not be put on stream in December if tests' results showed the metal was not safe and then power cuts would be introduced.
"In this case we will have to impose restrictions," Kuzmanov told Bulgaria's parliamentary energy committee late on Wednesday.

Preliminary results from the analysis of the vessel's metal of reactor number one are expected at the beginning of November and if they prove the reactor's safety it will be restarted at the beginning of December, he said.

Bulgaria's overstretched energy industry has been forced to ration electricity supplies since 1978 until 1973, relying on all the six reactors in Kozloduy's 3,760-megawatt plant and on its coal-fired thermal plants to meet the power needs.
Bulgaria imports 80 percent of its energy resources and currently suffers an acute economic crisis.

Earlier this week the central bank put nine ailing banks under special supervision and raised the interest rate to a record high of 300 percent in a bid to stabilise the country's wrecked financial system.
Another problem for the Kozloduy plant is its fresh fuel supplies from Russia due to a lack of funds, which delayed the recharging of the 1,000-megawatt reactor number six, officials said.
However, fuel will be supplied by air from October 2 and the reactor will be restarted at the beginning of November, Kuzmanov said.

Bulgaria, which produces mainly lignite coal, has contracted 700,000 tonnes of better quality coal from Vietnam for the Varna coal and gas-fired plant, which did not run last winter due to a lack of funds for coal.
The NEC has also agreed some Ukranian coal deliveries, Kuzmanov said, but did not give further details.
The 1,260-megawatt Varna plant is expected to help replace the electricity production from the closed Kozloduy reactor.
In July the European Union said it would grant 10 million Ecus to Bulgaria's energy sector as compensation for closing the controversial reactor and buying coal for the Varna plant.
